items.title: Max Balegde: how influencer turned a cunning comms plan into a No 10 nightmare
items.desc: Backlash to a single video overshadows Andy Burnham’s attempt to connect with hard-to-reach audiences When excited content creators gathered in the opulent surroundings of 10 Downing Street earlier this month, their mingling and poses in front of a Glambot camera were interrupted by a warm welcome from the prime minister. After showing the 60 or so gathered content creators a video of his own Instagram reel bloopers, Andy Burnham explained that he too had faced criticism for his prolific social media content. But, said the enthusiastic member of the creator ranks, he would continue because he was trying to reach people “where they were at”. Continue reading...

items.title: Poundland collapses, putting more than 10,000 jobs at risk

Tell us how you’re affected Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting more than 10,000 jobs at risk in “devastating news” for staff in the run-up to Christmas. Administrators at AlixPartners have been appointed to the retailer, which has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, by Poundland’s directors. The chain is now expected to be broken up, with significant job losses and store closures after its owners rejected at least two last-ditch bids for the budget retailer. Continue reading...

items.title: Cop31 collapse must be a catalyst for genuine climate action | Letters
items.desc: Readers on the failure of the climate talks in Turkey and the lessons we can learn The failure of Cop31, as commented on by Bill McGuire ( A year of deadly floods and fires – and yet Cop31 still collapsed. When will our leaders grasp the scale of this crisis?, 24 November ), is the expression of the overwhelming momentum of the value system of a global culture that is wedded to the seemingly unstoppable expansion of our material production and consumption. The disjunction between peril and necessary action is explained by the impossibility of taming appetites that are insatiable. It is convenient to blame fossil fuel producers, and while they are obviously guilty parties, the ultimate problem is the continuing demand for their products. Continue reading...

Eight in 10 Reform supporters think that asylum seekers are prioritised for social housing, compared with 21% of Green supporters. items.title: Brussels on split-screen: where it flexes – and where it bends
items.desc: From a choreographed summit that dominated Westminster but barely registered in Brussels to a climate showdown in Turkey, last week revealed the EU’s priorities – and the limits of its collective power • Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here Two very different European diplomatic dramas played out almost simultaneously last week. On Friday, a tightly choreographed EU-UK summit transfixed London, while barely registering on the continent. On Sunday, Cop31 collapsed after a united EU forcefully vetoed a watered-down climate pact, even as it relaxed its own green rules at home. What do these two events reveal about the EU: how it works, what takes up its bandwidth, how it exercises its clout – and where it’s vulnerable? *** Continue reading...

items.title: Energy bills jump: how to switch providers and is it worth it?
items.desc: It is possible to switch to a better tariff and save money despite the 26% price rise in January Average energy bill in Great Britain predicted to rise to £2,166 The energy price cap in Great Britain will go up by 26% in January to the equivalent of £2,166 a year. However, your bills might not have to rise by the same amount. If you are paying a tariff that matches the price cap you could save by switching to something lower. And if you do it now, you could make a substantial saving. On Wednesday, the cheapest fixed tariff on the market, an 18-month fix from Fuse Energy, was priced at £1,754 for an average home – £412 below the new January cap. It’s worth noting that it’s the price of the energy you use that is fixed, not your bill – so you will still be charged according to what you use. Continue reading...

items.title: Middle-aged women in England least likely to successfully quit smoking, study finds
items.desc: Of nearly 8,000 women who tried to stop, only 18% of those aged 45 to 60 managed to give up Middle-aged women in England are the least likely to successfully give up smoking, according to research . Smoking is the leading cause of preventable death and illness in the UK. While overall smoking rates in England have declined in recent decades, rates in some regions have increased. items.title: Latest review of Met police culture finds little has changed since last one
items.desc: Failure to implement previous reports means institutional racism, misogyny and homophobia still present in force Metropolitan police still institutionally racist and misogynist, says report From the Stephen Lawrence inquiry in 1999 to Louise Casey’s landmark review in 2023, successive reports on the Metropolitan police have arrived at the same damning conclusion: Britain’s largest police force is institutionally racist. It will, therefore, come as little surprise that three years after Casey’s report, an independent review led by Gillian Fairfield has found that institutional racism, misogyny and homophobia persist within the force. items.title: England has largest frailty gap out of 31 countries, study finds
items.desc: People from lowest socioeconomic group in all countries studied had higher frailty scores than those in highest socioeconomic group England has the largest gap between higher and lower socioeconomic groups when it comes to frailty compared with 30 other countries, a major study has found. The research, led by academics at King’s College London and published in BMC Medicine, looked at levels of frailty in 71,703 people from 31 countries including England, the US, China, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Sweden, Greece, Cyprus, Latvia and Lithuania.
